analysis.one_liner: Restores rules barring internet providers from blocking, slowing, or charging extra for websites.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 232-190, with every Democrat and one Republican voting yes, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would roll back the Federal Communications Commission's 2017 decision to stop regulating broadband companies like AT&T and Comcast as common carriers. It would reinstate the FCC's 2015 'net neutrality' rules, which prohibit internet providers from blocking lawful websites, slowing traffic to favor some services, or charging websites extra for faster delivery. It would also order studies on broadband competition, rural access, and how the rules affect communities with less internet access.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users, who get a legal guarantee that their provider cannot block, slow down, or prioritize websites based on who paid. Small websites, startups, and streaming services also benefit because they cannot be charged extra for fast delivery or pushed into slow lanes.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits internet providers from blocking lawful content, throttling (deliberately slowing) traffic, and selling 'paid prioritization' that lets some websites buy faster delivery than others.
Restores the FCC's authority over broadband by reclassifying mobile and fixed internet service as 'telecommunications services,' a legal category that lets the FCC enforce those rules.
Repeals the FCC's 2017 order that removed those rules and bars the FCC from reissuing substantially the same order without new authorization from Congress.

Gives broadband providers with 100,000 or fewer subscribers a one-year exemption from some disclosure requirements, and orders reports on broadband competition, accurate coverage maps, standalone (unbundled) broadband plans, and access on tribal lands, where only about 53% of residents have high-speed service.

analysis.who_pays: Large broadband providers like cable and telephone companies, which would lose the ability to block, slow, or prioritize traffic, and would face utility-style FCC regulation of their networks.

drawbacks.text: Opponents, including the broadband industry and most congressional Republicans, argued that treating broadband as a heavily regulated utility under rules written for 1930s telephone service would raise compliance costs and discourage investment in network upgrades, especially in rural areas.

The bill works by restoring a specific 2015 agency order verbatim rather than writing a new net neutrality law, so the rules' permanence depends on the FCC's legal authority rather than on a statute passed by both chambers.
The one-year exemption for small providers from certain transparency rules only defers, and does not resolve, the question of whether compliance costs fall harder on small internet providers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the trade-off is favorable: the bill guarantees that internet providers cannot charge websites for faster delivery or slow down competitors, protections most consumers already assumed they had. The main cost falls on broadband providers, though opponents' warning that stricter regulation would slow network investment is a serious argument that the record in these sources does not resolve. The bill's weakness is method: it reinstates an old agency order instead of writing a durable law, leaving the rules exposed to being reversed again whenever the FCC's majority changes.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill in April 2019, but the Senate put it on its calendar and never brought it up for a vote, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 8, 2019, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
It cleared the Communications and Technology subcommittee 18-11 and was ordered reported by the full committee 30-22, largely along party lines.
On April 10, 2019, the House passed the bill 232-190: all 231 voting Democrats voted yes, while only 1 of 197 Republicans did.
A Republican motion to recommit the bill with instructions failed 204-216, with 13 Democrats joining all 191 voting Republicans.
The Senate received the bill on April 11, 2019, and placed it on its legislative calendar on April 29, 2019; it was never scheduled for a floor vote.
Because the bill never became law, the FCC's 2017 order removing the net neutrality rules remained in effect through the end of that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major broadband providers are better off: the 2017 deregulation they favored stayed in place, and they faced no new blocking, throttling, or paid-prioritization rules during that Congress.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage every one of the 231 voting Democrats voted yes and just 1 of 197 Republicans did; the committee votes were 18-11 and 30-22 along the same lines.

industries.industry: Broadband internet providers (cable, telephone, and wireless carriers)
industries.note: The bill would bar them from blocking websites, slowing traffic, and selling paid priority to deep-pocketed sites, and would return them to FCC utility-style regulation. Their gain under the status quo (keeping the 2017 deregulation) is the public's loss of enforceable open-internet protections.

industries.industry: Websites, streaming services, and online startups
industries.note: They could not be charged extra for fast delivery or pushed into slow lanes, so they compete on content rather than on payments to internet providers — which also keeps costs from being passed to users.

The bill grants providers with up to 100,000 subscribers a one-year exemption from some disclosure requirements, easing their compliance burden while subjecting them to the same anti-blocking and anti-throttling rules as large carriers.
